Where it began

Cheteshwar Pujara was born in Rajkot, in Gujarat, on 25 January 1988, into a cricketing household. His father Arvind and his uncle Bipin had both played Ranji Trophy cricket for Saurashtra, and it was with his father that the young Cheteshwar did his early practice. He was 13 before he first played with a leather ball, and he later took a business degree at J. J. Kundalia College.

He arrived quickly once he did. Opening for India's Under-19 side against England in 2005, he made 211, and at the 2006 Under-19 World Cup he scored 349 runs and was named player of the tournament. His first-class debut for Saurashtra had come in December 2005.

The player

His Test career opened at Bangalore in October 2010 against Australia, and in his second innings he was sent in at three and made 72 as India chased 207. That number three spot became his home. He played 103 Tests from 2010 to 2023, scoring 7,195 runs at 43.61 with 19 hundreds and 35 fifties, and his best was the unbeaten 206 that set up victory over England at Ahmedabad in 2012.

The series people talk about most came in Australia in 2018–19. He made three hundreds, faced 1,258 balls and scored 521 runs, more than anyone on either side, and was player of the series as India won a Test series there for the first time.

What made him special

Patience was his craft. At Ranchi in 2017 he batted for 525 balls on his way to 202, at the time the longest Test innings by an Indian in balls faced, and early that year his first-class tally for the season reached 1,605, one more than the Indian record Chandu Borde had set in 1964–65. He was the ninth man to make three first-class triple hundreds, and by November 2017 he had made twelve first-class double hundreds, more than any Indian before him. In 2017 he climbed to second in the world Test batting rankings.

He was never a man for a hurry. In 2021 at the Gabba his fifty took 196 balls, and he played just 5 one-day internationals. The bowlers who spent whole afternoons trying to get him out would say that was rather the point.

Away from the middle

England's counties took to him. He turned out for Derbyshire, Yorkshire, Nottinghamshire and Sussex, and in July 2022 he marked his first match as Sussex captain with a hundred against Middlesex. At home he was part of the Chennai Super Kings squad that won the IPL in 2021. He received the Arjuna Award and was named Emerging Cricketer of the Year for 2013.

In June 2025 he joined the BBC's Test Match Special team as an analyst, and on 24 August 2025 he retired from all cricket.

And finally

For a batsman so happy to stay put, he did a good deal of running. In 2018 he was run out four times in Tests, which matched a record held by Australia's Bill Lawry for 54 years. Even his dismissals took some getting.
